channel.title: Pi Stack
channel.description: Comprehensive guides for open source alternatives, self-hosted software, privacy tools, and local AI deployment. Expert comparisons, setup guides, and benchmarks.

item.title: Erlang/OTP Concurrency in 2026: gen_server vs gen_statem vs poolboy vs gproc
item.description: Your Erlang service has been up for eleven days, memory is climbing, and erlang:process_info(Pid, message_queue_len) returns 1.8 million. One gen_server is doing database work inline, every caller is queued behind it, and the node is one OOM killer away from a restart. Nothing in the language stopped you — the BEAM happily lets you build a single-process bottleneck and call it architecture.

item.title: Haskell Streaming Libraries in 2026: conduit vs pipes vs streamly
item.description: Your nightly ETL job reads a 40 GB CSV export, and readFile plus length sends the machine into swap. That is the moment most Haskell teams discover that lazy ByteString is not a streaming abstraction — it is a promise the runtime may not keep. You need a library that guarantees constant memory, closes file handles deterministically, and lets you compose sources, transforms and sinks without hand-rolling bracket gymnastics.

item.title: MasterDnsVPN vs DNSTT vs SlipStream in 2026: Which DNS Tunnel Actually Survives a Hostile Network?
item.description: Your ISP blocks port 443 to anything that is not on its allowlist, UDP looks like it has been shaped into mush, and yet DNS still resolves — because if DNS broke, the whole network would break with it. That single fact is why DNS tunnels refuse to die. In 2026 the tooling around them changed dramatically: a Go implementation with resolver health checks and eight load-balancing modes, a Rust rewrite that moved the tunnel onto QUIC multipath, and the original research implementation that everything else is measured against.

item.title: Nim Async I/O in 2026: chronos vs asyncdispatch vs threadpool
item.description: You picked Nim because it compiles to a single static binary, runs at C speed, and still reads like Python. Then you added a second HTTP dependency and the build exploded: one library wants std/asyncdispatch, the other wants chronos, and the two Future types are not the same type. There is no adapter, no await bridge, and no compiler message that explains what went wrong.

item.title: Hister vs YaCy vs Stract in 2026: Which Self-Hosted Search Engine Is Actually Worth Running?
item.description: Search is the one utility almost nobody self-hosts, and the reason is a misunderstanding. People hear “self-hosted search engine” and assume they must out-crawl Google. They do not. The useful question is narrower: which of your own information should be searchable without a third party in the loop?

item.title: OmnySSH vs Voltius vs RustConn in 2026: Three Termius Alternatives That Don't Need a Subscription
item.description:
OmnySSH vs Voltius vs RustConn in 2026: Three Termius Alternatives That Don’t Need a Subscription

Termius sat at 649 MB of RAM across nine processes on an idle machine. That is not a typo, and it is not a benchmark run under load — it is what one of these projects measured while comparing itself to the incumbent. For a tool whose entire job is holding an SSH socket open, that is an absurd amount of memory, and it is exactly why the paid-SSH-client category has been quietly rebuilt in Rust over the last two years.

item.title: ProxCenter vs PegaProx vs Proxmox Datacenter Manager: Which Multi-Cluster Console Wins in 2026?
item.description:
ProxCenter vs PegaProx vs Proxmox Datacenter Manager: Which Multi-Cluster Console Wins in 2026?

You can run one Proxmox VE node from its built-in web UI forever. The moment you own three clusters in two racks — plus a Proxmox Backup Server — that same UI becomes a tab-hopping exercise in copy-pasting VMIDs. The stock interface has no concept of “all my infrastructure.” It shows one cluster at a time, and it shows it well, but it never shows you the whole estate.

item.title: RustFS vs VaultS3 vs Alarik in 2026: Three MinIO Alternatives That Fit in 200 MB of RAM
item.description:
RustFS vs VaultS3 vs Alarik in 2026: Three MinIO Alternatives That Fit in 200 MB of RAM

MinIO spent years as the default answer to “I need S3 on my own hardware.” Then its console and administrative capabilities started moving behind a commercial tier, and a lot of people who had built backup pipelines on the community edition discovered they were now renting back something they thought they owned. That is not a licensing debate — it is an operational risk that showed up in production for anyone running MinIO as the storage layer under Restic, Velero or Loki.

item.title: Self-Hosted Travel Planners in 2026: TREK vs Wanderer vs AdventureLog
item.description: You plan a two-week trip across four countries, and your entire itinerary lives inside a service that can change its pricing, shut down, or hand your location history to an advertiser. That is the actual trade you make with most travel apps. Self-hosting a trip planner flips it: your bookings, GPX tracks, budgets and photos stay on a box you control, and no company can decide your travel log is a data asset to monetize.

item.title: WAHA vs Evolution API vs WPPConnect in 2026: Which Self-Hosted WhatsApp API Survives Production?
item.description: Every WhatsApp integration starts the same way: a support inbox that needs to answer customers where they already are, and no budget for per-conversation messaging fees. Someone finds a self-hosted gateway on GitHub, it works in ten minutes, and three months later the number is banned and the integration is a liability.

item.title: Databasus vs pgBackRest vs pg_probackup: PostgreSQL Backup You Can Actually Prove (2026)
item.description: An untested backup is a rumour. The uncomfortable part of PostgreSQL operations is not taking the backup — pg_dump has worked for twenty years — it is proving that the backup restores, that the WAL stream has no gaps, and that the recovery point you promise your business is the recovery point you actually get. Three tools take three different routes to that proof: Databasus (9,196 stars), pgBackRest (4,458) and pg_probackup (799). One wraps backup in a web console with scheduled restore verification, one is the battle-tested CLI workhorse of the Postgres world, and one is Postgres Pro’s block-level incremental engine.

item.title: Komari vs CheckCle vs Beszel in 2026: Which Self-Hosted Server Monitor Actually Fits?
item.description: Your monitoring stack should not be heavier than the services it watches. That is the uncomfortable truth behind the latest wave of self-hosted monitors: teams abandoned Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager for a single VPS because the observability bill and the operational surface outgrew the workload. Komari (6,612 stars), CheckCle (3,309 stars) and Beszel (26,565 stars) attack that problem from three different angles — and picking the wrong one costs you either visibility or an afternoon of reverse-proxy debugging.

item.title: Microsandbox vs SmolVM vs smolBSD in 2026: Which MicroVM Sandbox Should Run Your Untrusted Code?
item.description: You just let a plugin system, a CI job, or a user-submitted script execute on your server. A container was supposed to contain it — except a container shares your kernel, and one kernel exploit later your “sandbox” is a shell on the host. Namespaces are an isolation convenience, not a security boundary. The boundary is a hypervisor, and in 2026 three projects make it cheap enough to use per-job instead of per-datacenter.

item.title: Scanopy vs Homelable vs Neko-Master: Self-Hosted Network Diagrams That Update Themselves (2026)
item.description: Every network diagram is a lie within about three weeks. You draw the VLANs, label the switch ports, screenshot it into the wiki — and then someone adds a Proxmox node, a test SSID appears on the AP, and the drawing becomes archaeology. Three self-hosted projects are attacking that decay from different directions: Scanopy (5,909 stars), Homelable (4,549) and Neko-Master (4,211) — one scans your subnets and redraws itself, one gives you a curated map with live status, and one turns raw traffic into a geographic picture of what your network is actually doing.

item.title: Scrapling vs Pydoll vs Scraperr in 2026: Which Scraping Stack Should You Self-Host?
item.description: Your scraper worked fine on Monday. By Thursday the site shipped a JavaScript bundle that renders everything client-side, your CSS selectors return null, and the requests loop that ran in 40 seconds now hangs for nine minutes before throwing a 403. Every data team hits this wall, and the usual reaction — bolt Selenium onto a Flask app and hope — is how you end up maintaining a browser farm instead of shipping data.

item.title: Termix vs Warpgate vs Sshwifty in 2026: Which Self-Hosted SSH Gateway Belongs in Your DMZ?
item.description: Somebody on your team is still SSH-ing into production from a laptop with a key that has never been rotated, through port 22 exposed to the internet, with no record of what they ran. You know it because you saw it in the audit. The fix is not a VPN — it is a gateway that authenticates the human, records the session, and forwards the connection to the target without ever giving the client network-level access.

item.title: Copyparty vs Dufs vs KodExplorer in 2026: Which Single-Binary File Server Should You Deploy?
item.description: You need to hand a folder of files to eight people across three networks. Nextcloud wants a database, a PHP-FPM pool, a Redis instance, a cron daemon, and roughly 700 MB of RAM before it will serve a single byte — and that is before the “it says my upload failed at 94%” support tickets start. Sometimes the right answer is not a collaboration suite. It is a file server that is one process, one config, and one open port.

item.title: Embassy vs RTIC vs esp-hal in 2026: Which Async Runtime Should Run Your Embedded Rust?
item.description: Firmware written with a bare superloop plus a handful of interrupt handlers has a predictable failure mode: at 40 MHz everything works, and at 400 kHz of event traffic two handlers start corrupting the same state machine. The classic fix — a real-time operating system — costs you a scheduler tick, a heap, and a debugger workflow that no longer matches the silicon. Rust’s answer is different: keep the single stack, drop the RTOS, and get concurrency from async plus compile-time priority analysis.

item.title: Lobsters vs Misago vs FlaskBB in 2026: Lightweight Self-Hosted Forums That Skip the 2 GB Tax
item.description: The standard advice for “I need a forum” is Discourse. The standard outcome is a 2 GB RAM bill, two containers, a Redis instance, and a Sidekiq process — for a community of 400 people discussing bicycle routes. Discourse is excellent software aimed at large communities with paid ops staff. It is also wildly oversized for a club, a product’s user base, an internal Q&A board, or a research group.

item.title: SVGO vs svgcleaner vs Scour in 2026: Which SVG Optimizer Actually Shrinks Your Assets?
item.description: Your designer exports a 14 KB logo from Figma. Your build ships it as a 14 KB logo, plus 60 % of that file is editor metadata, unused defs, and decimal coordinates with six digits. Multiply that by the 200 icons in your design system and you have shipped a megabyte of XML that nobody wrote and nobody reviews.
